- If sentiment shows a sharp upward spike followed by a drop, model tends to overreact and overshoot — reduce forecast peak by 5–10%.
- When sentiment change is negative and news volume is high, model often undercorrects — adjust downward by 2–5% to align with mean reversion.
- If recent sentiment is consistently positive (e.g., >0.67) and model forecast is rising, check for lag — true price often peaks 1–2 days later; delay forecast by 1–2 days if sentiment is trending up.
- If sentiment is flat or negative and model is rising, model overestimates recovery — reduce forecast by 3–7% to avoid overconfidence in low-sentiment periods.
- When news volume is low and sentiment is volatile, model tends to overfit short-term noise — apply smoothing filter or reduce forecast volatility by 15–20%.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome over 3–5 days, apply downward bias correction — subtract 1–3% per day to reflect mean reversion.
- If sentiment change is positive and news volume is high, model often overestimates momentum — reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid “sentiment-driven overhang.”
